claim: Penicillin and related antibiotics disrupt cell wall synthesis in bacteria causing the downstream misactivation of cell wall hydrolases called autolysins to induce cell lysis.
source: Penicillin and related antibiotics disrupt cell wall synthesis in bacteria causing the downstream misactivation of cell wall hydrolases called autolysins to induce cell lysis.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about how penicillin and related antibiotics work, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: In the pathogen Streptococcus pneumoniae (Sp), LytA is the major autolysin responsible for penicillin-induced bacteriolysis.
source: In the pathogen Streptococcus pneumoniae (Sp), LytA is the major autolysin responsible for penicillin-induced bacteriolysis.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work (Tomasz and Waks, 1975; Tomasz et al., 1970) mentioned in the introduction.

claim: Penicillin treatment of Sp causes a dramatic shift in surface polymer biogenesis in which cell wall-anchored teichoic acids (WTAs) increase in abundance at the expense of lipid-linked teichoic acids (LTAs).
source: We recently discovered that penicillin treatment of Sp causes a dramatic shift in surface polymer biogenesis in which cell wall-anchored teichoic acids (WTAs) increase in abundance at the expense of lipid-linked teichoic acids (LTAs).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work (Flores-Kim et al., 2019) and is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: LytA binds to both WTAs and LTAs.
source: Because LytA binds to both species of teichoic acids, this change recruits the enzyme to its substrate where it cleaves the cell wall and elicits lysis.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about LytA's choline-binding properties and citations in the text.

claim: The shift in WTA/LTA balance recruits LytA to the cell wall where it cleaves the cell wall and elicits lysis.
source: Because LytA binds to both species of teichoic acids, this change recruits the enzyme to its substrate where it cleaves the cell wall and elicits lysis.
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference based on the authors' previous findings (Flores-Kim et al., 2019).

claim: WhyD is a WTA hydrolase that restricts the WTA content of the wall to areas adjacent to active peptidoglycan (PG) synthesis.
source: We show that WhyD is a WTA hydrolase that restricts the WTA content of the wall to areas adjacent to active peptidoglycan (PG) synthesis.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by biochemical data in Figure 3 and localization data in Figure 7.

claim: The WTA tailoring activity of WhyD during exponential growth directs PG remodeling activity required for proper cell elongation.
source: Our results support a model in which the WTA tailoring activity of WhyD during exponential growth directs PG remodeling activity required for proper cell elongation in addition to preventing autolysis by LytA.
evidence: This is a model supported by data showing morphological changes in cells with altered WhyD levels (Figures 4 and 5).

claim: The PG layer is a continuous matrix that requires the activity of enzymes that cut bonds in the network called PG hydrolases or autolysins.
source: Since the PG layer is a continuous matrix, cell wall biogenesis also requires the activity of enzymes that cut bonds in the network called PG hydrolases or autolysins.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field supported by multiple citations.

claim: PG hydrolases are important for breaking bonds in the matrix to allow for its expansion and the insertion of new material into the pre-existing meshwork.
source: These space-making factors are important for breaking bonds in the matrix to allow for its expansion and the insertion of new material into the pre-existing meshwork (Bisicchia et al., 2007; Carballido-López et al., 2006; Dobihal et al., 2019; Dörr et al., 2013; Meisner et al., 2013; Singh et al., 2012; Sycuro et al., 2010; Vollmer et al., 2008; Wilson and Garner, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: PG hydrolases play important roles in cleaving shared cell wall material connecting daughter cells during cytokinesis.
source: They also play important roles in cleaving shared cell wall material connecting daughter cells during cytokinesis (Hashimoto et al., 2018; Heidrich et al., 2002; Vollmer et al., 2008; Wilson and Garner, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: β-lactams and related antibiotics kill bacteria by corrupting the activity of PG hydrolases to damage the cell wall and cause catastrophic lysis.
source: Notably, β-lactams and related antibiotics have long been known to kill bacteria by corrupting the activity of PG hydrolases to damage the cell wall and cause catastrophic lysis (Cho et al., 2014; Salamaga et al., 2021; Tomasz and Waks, 1975; Tomasz et al., 1970).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Streptococcus pneumoniae only requires a single autolysin, LytA, to trigger its characteristic growth-phase-dependent and antibiotic-induced lysis phenotypes.
source: To circumvent this difficulty, we used the gram-positive pathogen Streptococcus pneumoniae (Sp) because it only requires a single autolysin, LytA, to trigger its characteristic growth-phase-dependent and antibiotic-induced lysis phenotypes (Tomasz and Waks, 1975; Tomasz et al., 1970).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A Tn-Seq screen for factors that control LytA activity revealed that LytA regulation is intimately linked to the biogenesis of surface glycopolymers called teichoic acids (TAs).
source: The screen revealed that LytA regulation is intimately linked to the biogenesis of surface glycopolymers called teichoic acids (TAs) (Flores-Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work.

claim: In Sp cells, both LTAs and WTAs are made from a common precursor linked to the lipid carrier undecaprenyl phosphate (Und-P).
source: In Sp cells, both types of TAs are made from a common precursor linked to the lipid carrier undecaprenyl phosphate (Und-P) (Brown et al., 2013; Denapaite et al., 2012; Fischer et al., 1993; Gisch et al., 2013; Heß et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: LTAs and WTAs in Sp are decorated with choline moieties, which serve as binding sites for LytA and other Sp enzymes with choline-binding domains (CBDs).
source: They are also decorated with choline moieties, which serve as binding sites for LytA and other Sp enzymes with choline-binding domains (CBDs) (Brown et al., 2013; Denapaite et al., 2012; Fischer et al., 1993; Gisch et al., 2013; Heß et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: During exponential growth, LTAs predominate and sequester LytA at the membrane thereby preventing cell wall damage.
source: We previously found that during exponential growth, LTAs predominate and sequester LytA at the membrane thereby preventing cell wall damage (Flores-Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work.

claim: Upon antibiotic treatment or upon prolonged periods in stationary phase, the membrane protease FtsH degrades the LTA synthase TacL, causing a dramatic decrease in LTA levels, and an increase in WTAs.
source: However, upon antibiotic treatment or upon prolonged periods in stationary phase, the membrane protease FtsH degrades the LTA synthase TacL, causing a dramatic decrease in LTA levels, and an increase in WTAs.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work (Flores-Kim et al., 2019).

claim: The switch in TA polymer abundance leads to the relocalization of LytA from the membrane to the cell wall where its cleavage activity compromises wall integrity, inducing lysis.
source: This switch in TA polymer abundance leads to the relocalization of LytA from the membrane to the cell wall where its cleavage activity compromises wall integrity, inducing lysis (Flores-Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work.

claim: In wild-type (WT) cells, relatively few transposon insertions were mapped in whyD, consistent with previous genomic studies that reported it to be an essential gene.
source: In wild-type (WT) cells, relatively few transposon insertions were mapped in whyD, consistent with previous genomic studies that reported it to be an essential gene (Liu et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2021; van Opijnen and Camilli, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by Tn-Seq data shown in Figure 1A and citations to previous genomic studies.

claim: In cells lacking LytA, insertions in whyD were readily detected.
source: By contrast, in cells lacking LytA, insertions in whyD were readily detected (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by Tn-Seq data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: When LytA was absent (no inducer), cells were viable in the presence or absence of whyD.
source: When LytA was absent (no inducer), cells were viable in the presence or absence of whyD (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by spot dilution data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: When LytA was expressed (+Zn), viability was severely compromised only in cells deleted for whyD.
source: However, when LytA was expressed (+Zn), viability was severely compromised only in cells deleted for whyD (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by spot dilution data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: LytA production in cells lacking WhyD during growth in liquid medium caused premature lysis in late exponential phase.
source: Furthermore, LytA production in cells lacking WhyD during growth in liquid medium caused premature lysis in late exponential phase (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Addition of rLytA to a ΔlytA mutant during exponential growth restored the stationary phase autolysis phenotype exhibited by WT cells.
source: Addition of rLytA to a ΔlytA mutant during exponential growth restored the stationary phase autolysis phenotype exhibited by WT cells whereas its addition to a ΔlytA ΔwhyD double mutant resulted in lysis almost immediately after exposure (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Addition of rLytA to a ΔlytA ΔwhyD double mutant resulted in lysis almost immediately after exposure.
source: Addition of rLytA to a ΔlytA mutant during exponential growth restored the stationary phase autolysis phenotype exhibited by WT cells whereas its addition to a ΔlytA ΔwhyD double mutant resulted in lysis almost immediately after exposure (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In mutants defective for TacL, LTAs were undetectable and WTA levels dramatically increased.
source: As a control, we analyzed LTA and WTA levels in mutants inactivated for the LTA synthase TacL. As expected, LTAs were undetectable in these cells and WTA levels dramatically increased (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot and gel data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In mutants defective for WhyD, a dramatic increase in WTAs was observed.
source: In mutants defective for WhyD, a similarly dramatic increase in WTAs was observed.
evidence: This is supported by gel data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In whyD mutants, LTA levels were unaffected.
source: However, in this case, LTA levels were unaffected (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Expression of whyD from an ectopic locus restored WT levels of WTAs.
source: Expression of whyD from an ectopic locus restored WT levels of WTAs, indicating that the phenotype was due to the absence of the WhyD protein rather than an effect of the deletion on the expression of a nearby gene (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by gel data shown in Figure 2.

claim: WhyD protein levels remained unchanged during exponential growth and under autolytic conditions.
source: However, unlike TacL, WhyD protein levels remained unchanged during exponential growth and under autolytic conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating that the rise in WTA abundance in the stationary phase or following penicillin treatment does not involve the degradation of WhyD.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The change in WTA/LTA abundance under autolytic conditions was found to be unaffected by WhyD inactivation.
source: Additionally, the change in WTA/LTA abundance under autolytic conditions was found to be unaffected by WhyD inactivation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: WhyD is required to prevent LytA-induced autolysis during exponential growth by limiting the accumulation of WTAs in the cell wall.
source: Although further work will be required to determine how WhyD activity is inhibited during the induction of autolysis, the results thus far clearly indicate that WhyD is required to prevent LytA-induced autolysis during exponential growth by limiting the accumulation of WTAs in the cell wall.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The whyD gene encodes a protein with seven predicted N-terminal transmembrane segments followed by an extracellular GlpQ phosphodiesterase domain.
source: The whyD gene encodes a protein with seven predicted N-terminal transmembrane segments followed by an extracellular GlpQ phosphodiesterase domain (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Proteins with the GlpQ domain from Bacillus subtilis and Staphylococcus aureus have been shown to hydrolyze WTAs.
source: Proteins with this domain from Bacillus subtilis and Staphylococcus aureus have recently been shown to hydrolyze WTAs (Jorge et al., 2018; Myers et al., 2016; Walter et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: WhyDCT released WTAs from sacculi into the supernatant.
source: As anticipated, WhyDCT, but not buffer alone, released WTAs from sacculi into the supernatant (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: WTA release by WhyDCT was inhibited by the addition of the chelator EDTA.
source: Similarly, we found that WTA release by WhyDCT was inhibited by the addition of the chelator EDTA.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: WhyDCT was unable to release LTAs from purified membranes.
source: Consistent with our in vivo data showing that inactivation of WhyD has no effect on the abundance of LTAs (Figure 2), WhyDCT was unable to release LTAs from purified membranes (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: WhyD functions as a WTA hydrolase in Sp cells.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that WhyD functions as a WTA hydrolase in Sp cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the biochemical data in Figure 3.

claim: Cells lacking WhyD were found to be longer, wider, and overall larger.
source: Cells lacking WhyD were found to be longer, wider, and overall larger (Figure 4A and B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy and quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4A, B, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Overexpression of whyD (whyD++), which lowers WTA abundance to nearly undetectable levels, reduced cell length and overall cell size.
source: Conversely, overexpression of whyD (whyD++), which lowers WTA abundance to nearly undetectable levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), reduced cell length and overall cell size (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy, quantitative analysis, and biochemical data shown in Figure 4C-E and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: WhyD and WTAs are important for normal cell elongation.
source: These results argue that WhyD and WTAs are important for normal cell elongation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the morphological data in Figure 4.

claim: Mutants lacking LytA, LytB, and LytC (ΔlytABC) displayed a cell separation defect.
source: Consistent with other reports and the function of LytB as the main Sp cell separation PG hydrolase, ΔlytABC cells displayed a cell separation defect (Figure 5A; De Las Rivas et al., 2002; Zucchini et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5A and citations to previous work.

claim: Cells within the ΔlytABC chains were shorter and overall smaller than WT, indicative of an elongation defect.
source: However, like cells with reduced WTA levels, the cells within the ΔlytABC chains were also shorter and overall smaller than WT, indicative of an elongation defect (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Sp cells likely employ WhyD to maintain a level of WTAs in the wall that are low enough to prevent autolysis but sufficient to allow WTA-binding hydrolases to promote PG expansion and cytokinesis.
source: We therefore infer that Sp cells likely employ WhyD to maintain a level of WTAs in the wall that are low enough to prevent autolysis but sufficient to allow WTA-binding hydrolases to promote PG expansion and cytokinesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: A fusion of GFP to the N-terminus of WhyD (GFP-WhyD) without a linker between the two proteins was fluorescent and stable enough to complement the ΔwhyD mutant phenotype.
source: However, a fusion of GFP to the N-terminus of WhyD (GFP-WhyD) without a linker between the two proteins was fluorescent and stable enough to complement the ΔwhyD mutant phenotype (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by complementation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Exponentially growing cells displayed an enrichment of GFP-WhyD at midcell that co-localized with the HADA signal.
source: Nevertheless, an enrichment of GFP-WhyD at midcell was observable that co-localized with the HADA signal (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: WhyD is recruited to areas of nascent PG synthesis at midcell.
source: These data suggest that WhyD is recruited to areas of nascent PG synthesis at midcell.
evidence: This is an inference based on the localization data in Figure 6.

claim: rLytA-Alexa triggered growth phase-dependent autolysis at rates indistinguishable from unlabeled rLytA.
source: Importantly, rLytA-Alexa triggered growth phase-dependent autolysis at rates indistinguishable from unlabeled rLytA (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), indicating that labeling did not affect LytA activity.
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Surface labeling by rLytA*-Alexa was undetectable when WhyD was overexpressed (+Zn).
source: However, rLytA*-Alexa was undetectable when WhyD was overexpressed (+Zn) (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: rLytA*-Alexa exclusively labels WTAs when added to intact cells.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that rLytA*-Alexa specifically binds WTAs when added to intact cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data in Figure 7—figure supplements 1-3.

claim: Elongating cells displayed a weak rLytA*-Alexa signal at midcell that co-localized with sBADA.
source: Elongating cells displayed a weak rLytA*-Alexa signal at midcell that co-localized with sBADA.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The sBADA signal at midcell was flanked by two prominent fluorescent bands of rLytA*-Alexa that co-localized with HADA-labeled peripheral PG.
source: The sBADA signal at midcell was flanked by two prominent fluorescent bands of rLytA*-Alexa that co-localized with HADA-labeled peripheral PG (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: In cells nearing the completion of cell division, rLytA*-Alexa and HADA co-localized within the deep cell constrictions.
source: In cells nearing the completion of cell division, the pattern changed with rLytA*-Alexa and HADA co-localizing within the deep cell constrictions (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplements 5 and 6).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplements 5 and 6.

claim: rLytA*-Alexa was present throughout the PG matrix in cells lacking WhyD.
source: In support of the idea that WhyD is responsible for promoting the observed WTA localization, rLytA*-Alexa was present throughout the PG matrix in cells lacking WhyD (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: WhyD removes most, but not all, WTAs from nascent PG at midcell, resulting in low levels of WTAs being incorporated in the peripheral PG that brackets the septum.
source: Altogether, these results support a model (Figure 8) in which WhyD removes most, but not all, WTAs from nascent PG at midcell, resulting in low levels of WTAs being incorporated in the peripheral PG that brackets the septum.
evidence: This is a model based on the data in Figure 7.

claim: The localization of WTAs likely allows the recruitment of PG hydrolases to the peripheral region to promote the zonal expansion of the cell wall for elongation.
source: This localization of WTAs likely allows the recruitment of PG hydrolases to the peripheral region to promote the zonal expansion of the cell wall for elongation.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the data.

claim: The change in WTA localization to deep constrictions in late-divisional cells is consistent with the role for the polymers in recruitment of LytB and other choline-binding PG hydrolases to catalyze the last stage of cell separation.
source: Similarly, the change in WTA localization to deep constrictions in late-divisional cells is consistent with the role for the polymers in recruitment of LytB and other choline-binding PG hydrolases to catalyze the last stage of cell separation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data in Figure 7 and established knowledge about LytB function.

claim: Localized pruning of WTAs from nascent PG by WhyD provides a mechanism by which Sp can direct the activity of its PG hydrolases to facilitate growth and division of the PG matrix.
source: Thus, localized pruning of WTAs from nascent PG by WhyD provides a mechanism by which Sp can direct the activity of its PG hydrolases to facilitate growth and division of the PG matrix (see Discussion).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the overall findings of the study.

claim: WTAs are required for normal cell growth and division in many gram-positive bacteria.
source: WTAs are required for normal cell growth and division in many gram-positive bacteria, and in several cases, these polymers have been implicated in controling the localization of PG hydrolases as part of their morphogenic function (Brown et al., 2013; Kasahara et al., 2016; Schlag et al., 2010; Zamakhaeva et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: WTA tailoring by the WhyD hydrolase plays an important role in control by promoting the localized accumulation of WTA polymers at sites adjacent to active areas of PG synthesis in Sp cells.
source: Here, we show that WTA tailoring by the WhyD hydrolase plays an important role in this control process by promoting the localized accumulation of WTA polymers at sites adjacent to active areas of PG synthesis in Sp cells.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the data presented.

claim: The pruning of WTAs prevents the excessive recruitment of the LytA PG hydrolase to the cell wall to avoid autolysis during exponential growth.
source: This pruning of WTAs prevents the excessive recruitment of the LytA PG hydrolase to the cell wall to avoid autolysis during exponential growth.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the data presented.

claim: The localization of WTAs promoted by WhyD functions to guide the activity of WTA-binding PG hydrolases to specific subcellular sites where they can promote the remodeling of the wall necessary for proper cell elongation and division.
source: Additionally, our results suggest that the localization of WTAs promoted by WhyD also functions to guide the activity of WTA-binding PG hydrolases to specific subcellular sites where they can promote the remodeling of the wall necessary for proper cell elongation and division.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the data presented.

claim: The continuous degradation of WTAs maintains their low levels in the cell wall of actively growing cells.
source: However, the discovery that WhyD inactivation also causes a dramatic increase in WTA accumulation in exponentially growing cells without affecting LTA accumulation (Figure 2) indicates that instead of substrate competition, it is likely that the continuous degradation of WTAs maintains their low levels in the cell wall of actively growing cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data in Figure 2.

claim: The enrichment of WhyD in the septal region is likely to result in the removal of most but not all WTAs added to nascent PG.
source: In this scenario, the enrichment of WhyD in the septal region is likely to result in the removal of most but not all WTAs added to nascent PG.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the localization data.

claim: Zonal PG synthesis would be expected to push the WTA-decorated PG material away from the cell center.
source: Zonal PG synthesis would then be expected to push the WTA-decorated PG material away from the cell center (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the model.

claim: The concentration of WTAs at late-stage septa is likely to promote the midcell recruitment of hydrolases to facilitate daughter cell separation.
source: As observed in other gram-positive bacteria, including Streptococcus mutans, the concentration of WTAs at late-stage septa is likely to promote the midcell recruitment of hydrolases to facilitate daughter cell separation (Zamakhaeva et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data and comparison to other bacteria.

claim: The viability of the ΔlytABC mutant suggests that there are additional space-making PG hydrolases in Sp cells.
source: Thus, either there are other WTA-binding PG hydrolases with a space-making function yet to be identified in Sp cells or WTAs have an essential function other than promoting cell wall expansion. In either case, the viability of the ΔlytABC mutant suggests that there are additional space-making PG hydrolases in Sp cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the viability of the ΔlytABC mutant.

claim: WhyD is unlikely to cleave within the WTA polymer itself.
source: However, because WTAs and LTAs in Sp cells are built from a common undecaprenyl-linked precursor and have an identical polymeric structure (Denapaite et al., 2012), WhyD is unlikely to cleave within the polymer itself.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural similarity of WTAs and LTAs.

claim: WhyD works as an endoenzyme, specifically cleaving the phosphate linkage between the WTA polymer and PG.
source: Given that the only major difference between WTAs in Sp cells relative to the precursor or the LTAs is its linkage to the PG (Brown et al., 2013; Denapaite et al., 2012; Fischer et al., 1993; Gisch et al., 2013; Heß et al., 2017), we favor a model in which WhyD works as an endoenzyme, specifically cleaving the phosphate linkage between the WTA polymer and PG.
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the biochemical data and structural knowledge.

claim: WhyDCT is unable to hydrolyze LTAs or the Und-P linked TA precursor.
source: In support of this idea, WhyDCT is unable to release TA polymers from membranes (Figure 3), indicating that it is unable to hydrolyze LTAs or the Und-P linked TA precursor.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical data in Figure 3C.

claim: It is possible that WTAs may be recycled in Sp cells in a manner similar to how PG turnover products are recycled in many bacterial species.
source: However, such a scenario is not that different from the synthesis of the cell wall itself, which has been reported to involve the turnover of up to 50% of the PG layer per generation in other bacteria (Borisova et al., 2016; Johnson et al., 2013). It is therefore possible that WTAs may be recycled in Sp cells in a manner similar to how PG turnover products are recycled in many bacterial species.
evidence: This is speculation based on comparison to PG recycling.

claim: The N-terminal multi-pass transmembrane domain of WhyD shares remote homology with a family of plasma-membrane choline transporters (PF04515).
source: Notably, the N-terminal multi-pass transmembrane domain of WhyD shares remote homology with a family of plasma-membrane choline transporters (PF04515), raising the intriguing possibility that this domain might function to import the WTA polymers cleaved by WhyDCT to recycle choline and other components of the polymers.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis and is speculative.

claim: Inactivation of choline-binding hydrolases other than LytA were unable to suppress whyD essentiality.
source: Inactivation of choline-binding hydrolase other than LytA were unable to suppress whyD essentiality (Supplementary file 1), indicating that the misactivation of other hydrolases does not play a major role in the lethal phenotype of the ∆whyD mutant.
evidence: This is supported by data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: B. subtilis mutants inactivated for GlpQ are hypersensitive to several β-lactam antibiotics.
source: Notably, B. subtilis mutants inactivated for GlpQ are hypersensitive to several β-lactam antibiotics (Myers et al., 2016), suggesting that WTA remodeling is generally important for controling autolysis in gram-positive bacteria.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: WhyD and other related GlpQ family members represent attractive targets for the development of new classes of lysis-inducing antibiotics and/or potentiators of existing β-lactam drugs.
source: Thus, WhyD and other related GlpQ family members represent attractive targets for the development of new classes of lysis-inducing antibiotics and/or potentiators of existing β-lactam drugs.
evidence: This is speculation about potential applications of the findings.

claim: WTAs can account for up to 30–50% of the dry weight of the cell wall in some gram-positive organisms like B. subtilis.
source: Additionally, in some gram-positive organisms like B. subtilis, WTAs can account for up to 30–50% of the dry weight of the cell wall (Brown et al., 2013; Ellwood, 1970).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In Sp cells, WTAs are kept at low levels during exponential phase via the activities of TacL and WhyD.
source: By contrast, in Sp cells, we find that WTAs are kept at low levels during exponential phase via the activities of TacL and WhyD (Flores-Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from the current and previous work.

claim: WTAs are essential in Sp.
source: Despite this low abundance and unlike most well-studied gram-positive bacteria, WTAs are essential in Sp (Johnsborg and Håvarstein, 2009; Ye et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: lytA inactivation had a small impact on cell size in comparison to WT.
source: We note that lytA inactivation had a small impact on cell size in comparison to WT, as observed previously (Barendt et al., 2011; De Las Rivas et al., 2002; Sanchez-Puelles et al., 1986; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and citations to previous work.

claim: Overexpression of whyD (whyD++) lowers WTA abundance to nearly undetectable levels.
source: Conversely, overexpression of whyD (whyD++), which lowers WTA abundance to nearly undetectable levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), reduced cell length and overall cell size (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical data in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The ΔlytABC mutant lacking all the known WTA-binding PG hydrolases produced during normal exponential growth is viable.
source: Although WTA biogenesis is essential in Sp cells in accordance with such a role in cell elongation, the ΔlytABC mutant lacking all the known WTA-binding PG hydrolases produced during normal exponential growth is viable.
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: GlpQ-containing proteins from B. subtilis and S. aureus function as WTA hydrolases.
source: GlpQ-containing proteins from other gram-positive bacteria like B. subtilis and S. aureus have been shown to function as WTA hydrolases (Jorge et al., 2018; Myers et al., 2016; Walter et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The previously characterized GlpQ-containing proteins are secreted and function to promote growth during phosphate-limitation.
source: Unlike WhyD, which is membrane-anchored and essential for normal growth, the previously characterized GlpQ-containing proteins are secreted and function to promote growth during phosphate-limitation (Jorge et al., 2018; Myers et al., 2016; Walter et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: B. subtilis GlpQ (BsGlpQ) acts as an exolytic enzyme that specifically degrades WTAs based on their distinct enantiomeric configuration relative to LTAs.
source: In B. subtilis (strain 168), LTAs and WTAs are both glycerolphosphate polymers, and B. subtilis GlpQ (BsGlpQ) has been shown to act as an exolytic enzyme that specifically degrades WTAs based on their distinct enantiomeric configuration relative to LTAs (Brown et al., 2013; Jorge et al., 2018; Myers et al., 2016; Walter et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: WhyD releases polymers from the wall with a length distribution that mirrors that of the LTAs.
source: Consistent with this idea, in contrast to BsGlpQ, which completely hydrolyzes its WTA substrate (Myers et al., 2016; Walter et al., 2020), WhyD releases polymers from the wall with a length distribution that mirrors that of the LTAs (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: WTAs are most efficiently attached to nascent PG before the newly synthesized glycans are crosslinked into the pre-existing meshwork.
source: Biochemical studies suggest that WTAs are most efficiently attached to nascent PG before the newly synthesized glycans are crosslinked into the pre-existing meshwork (Rausch et al., 2019; Schaefer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Orthologues of WhyDCT (GlpQ) in B. subtilis and S. aureus require Ca2+ ions for activity.
source: Orthologues of WhyDCT (GlpQ) in B. subtilis and S. aureus were previously shown to require Ca2+ ions for activity (Jorge et al., 2018; Myers et al., 2016; Walter et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Co-localization analysis of GFP-WhyD and WTAs showed an anti-correlation between GFP-WhyD enrichment at midcell and WTA localization.
source: Consistent with WhyD hydrolyzing WTAs at midcell, co-localization analysis of GFP-WhyD and WTAs showed an anti-correlation between GFP-WhyD enrichment at midcell and WTA localization (Figure 7—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 7—figure supplement 4.

claim: rLytA*-Alexa specifically labels Streptococcus pneumoniae cells but not Bacillus subtilis cells.
source: Furthermore, we confirmed that rLytA*-Alexa exclusively labels WTAs from Sp (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C) and purified Sp sacculi, provided that WTAs had not been removed (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: rLytA*-Alexa labels purified Sp sacculi only when WTAs are present.
source: Furthermore, we confirmed that rLytA*-Alexa exclusively labels WTAs from Sp (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C) and purified Sp sacculi, provided that WTAs had not been removed (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: Structured illumination microscopy (SIM) and image deconvolution analyses revealed rLytA*-Alexa localizing in regions offset from midcell in elongating cells and at deep constrictions in cells that have nearly completed division.
source: Structured illumination microscopy (SIM) and image deconvolution analyses revealed similar localization patterns with rLytA*-Alexa localizing in regions offset from midcell in elongating cells and at deep constrictions in cells that have nearly completed division (Figure 7—figure supplement 5C).
evidence: This is supported by SIM data in Figure 7—figure supplement 5C.

claim: Most bacterial cells are surrounded by a cell wall matrix composed of peptidoglycan (PG).
source: Most bacterial cells are surrounded by a cell wall matrix composed of peptidoglycan (PG).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The PG exoskeletal layer fortifies the cell membrane against internal osmotic pressure and is essential for cell integrity.
source: This exoskeletal layer fortifies the cell membrane against internal osmotic pressure and is essential for cell integrity.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The PG consists of glycan polymers with a repeating disaccharide unit of N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) and N-acetylmuramic acid (MurNAc).
source: The PG consists of glycan polymers with a repeating disaccharide unit of N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) and N-acetylmuramic acid (MurNAc).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Attached to the MurNAc sugar is a short peptide that is used to form crosslinks between adjacent glycan polymers, generating an interconnected PG matrix.
source: Attached to the MurNAc sugar is a short peptide that is used to form crosslinks between adjacent glycan polymers, generating an interconnected PG matrix.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Synthesis of the PG heteropolymer is mediated by the penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs), some of which possess both glycosyltransferase and transpeptidase activity needed to polymerize and crosslink the glycan strands of PG, respectively.
source: Synthesis of the PG heteropolymer is mediated by the penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs), some of which possess both glycosyltransferase and transpeptidase activity needed to polymerize and crosslink the glycan strands of PG, respectively (Goffin and Ghuysen, 1998; Sauvage et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The glycans are also polymerized by SEDS (shape, elongation, division and sporulation)-family proteins that work in unison with monofunctional PBPs possessing crosslinking activity.
source: The glycans are also polymerized by SEDS (shape, elongation, division and sporulation)-family proteins that work in unison with monofunctional PBPs possessing crosslinking activity (Cho et al., 2016; Emami et al., 2017; Meeske et al., 2016; Rohs et al., 2018; Sjodt et al., 2018; Taguchi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PBPs are the targets of penicillin and related β-lactam drugs.
source: Because PBPs are the targets of penicillin and related β-lactam drugs (Cho et al., 2014; Strominger and Tipper, 1965; Tipper and Strominger, 1965), much of the research focus in the field of cell wall biology has been on the regulation of cell wall synthesis by these enzymes and their inhibition by cell wall targeting antibiotics.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: TAs are major constituents of the gram-positive cell envelope and include both lipoteichoic acids (LTAs), which are membrane anchored, and wall teichoic acids (WTAs), which are covalently attached to the PG.
source: TAs are major constituents of the gram-positive cell envelope and include both lipoteichoic acids (LTAs), which are membrane anchored, and wall teichoic acids (WTAs), which are covalently attached to the PG (Brown et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Mutants defective in one or even several PG hydrolases rarely display a phenotype that can be exploited for genetic analysis of their regulation.
source: One of the main challenges in elucidating mechanisms controling PG hydrolase activity has been the genetic redundancy of these enzymes. Mutants defective in one or even several PG hydrolases rarely display a phenotype that can be exploited for genetic analysis of their regulation.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The reliance on a single enzyme for lysis induction allowed the design of a transposon sequencing (Tn-Seq) screen for factors that control LytA activity based on the identification of essential genes that become dispensable when LytA is inactivated.
source: This reliance on a single enzyme for lysis induction allowed us to design a transposon sequencing (Tn-Seq) screen for factors that control LytA activity based on the identification of essential genes that become dispensable when LytA is inactivated.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: whyD displayed a pattern of essentiality/non-essentiality expected for a LytA regulator in the Tn-Seq screen.
source: In addition to tacL described in our original report, we found that the whyD (spd_0880) gene also displayed a pattern of essentiality/non-essentiality expected for a LytA regulator (Figure 1A).

claim: A LytA-depletion strain was constructed in which the sole copy of lytA was under the control of a zinc-regulated promoter.
source: To validate the Tn-seq results, we constructed a LytA-depletion strain in which the sole copy of lytA was under the control of a zinc-regulated promoter (Eberhardt et al., 2009).
evidence: This describes a strain construction method used in the study.

claim: The sensitivity of the ΔwhyD strain to LytA activity could be recapitulated by the addition of purified recombinant LytA (rLytA) to cells.
source: Finally, the sensitivity of the ΔwhyD strain to LytA activity could be recapitulated by the addition of purified recombinant LytA (rLytA) to cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: whyD has the properties expected for a gene encoding a factor that restrains LytA activity at the cell surface.
